# Footnotes, Notes, and HTML {#chp:notes}

::: epigraph
> The devil is in the details.
>
> ---Proverb
:::

Every good table has fine print. A number needs a caveat, a column needs a
definition, a source needs credit. This chapter is about the small words that
sit around your table and make the big numbers trustworthy.

## Footnotes {#sec:footnote}

`lt_footnote()` hangs a numbered footnote on whatever you point at. The
`where` argument picks the target, and `columns`, `rows`, or `match` narrow it
down:

| `where`      | Attaches to               | Narrow it with            |
|--------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `"title"`    | the title                 | nothing                   |
| `"subtitle"` | the subtitle              | nothing                   |
| `"column"`   | a column label            | `columns`                 |
| `"spanner"`  | a spanner label           | `columns` (the spanner)   |
| `"group"`    | a row group label         | `match`                   |
| `"body"`     | specific cells            | `columns` and `rows`      |

Numbers go to footnotes in order of first appearance, so the count always runs
1, 2, 3 and never skips. Two footnotes with identical text share one number. The
example below uses all six targets at once, which is more footnotes than any
sensible table needs. Think of it as a stress test.

```{r, child = ex('footnote')}
```

::: callout-tip
Footnotes on body cells are the sharpest tool in the box. Use `rows` to point at
the exact cells that need the caveat, rather than footnoting a whole column that
is mostly fine.
:::

## Source notes {#sec:note}

A footnote explains one thing. A *note* sits in the footer and speaks for the
whole table: where the data came from, what was excluded, who to blame.
`lt_note()` adds an unnumbered line below any footnotes.

```{r, child = ex('note')}
```

Call it more than once to add more lines. Notes keep the order you gave them.

## HTML in cells and labels {#sec:html}

By default, lt treats every string as plain text and escapes it. That is a
feature: a stray `<` in your data will not break the page, and nobody can sneak
a `<script>` into a cell. But sometimes you really do want a link, some bold
text, or a superscript.

Two tools, two jobs:

- `lt_html()` marks whole *columns* as HTML. Use it when the data itself
  contains markup, like a column of links.
- `I()` marks a single *string* as raw HTML. Use it for titles, labels, and
  notes. (It is the base R "as is" wrapper, so there is nothing new to learn.)

```{r, child = ex('html')}
```

::: callout-warning
Raw HTML is passed through untouched. If the text comes from users you do not
trust, escape it first with `xfun::html_escape()`, or keep it out of
`lt_html()` columns altogether.
:::

With footnotes for the caveats, notes for the credits, and HTML for the
flourishes, the table now says everything it needs to. Next, let us make the
numbers speak in pictures: @chp:plots.
